meta.title: OUniverse fact check
meta.statusNote: Status is judged as of 14 October 2026.
meta.lede: A fact check of everything new or changed since 30 September, including today’s colleague comments and the nine new objects, plus statuses, numbers and flagged claims. Style rewrites put the OU text in the first person ("we") and make it shorter; accept them one by one.

c.q: Heading "Open University Involvement" above the OU text
c.note: If you accept the first-person rewrites, the heading reads oddly above "We…". Suggest "Our part in it" or "Our involvement". This is a code change in src/apps/showcase/details.js, made by hand.

e.from: Open University Involvement
e.to: Our involvement

c.q: Arrives at Didymos on 12 October 2026 (last waypoint)
c.note: ESA now says Hera arrives in November 2026, a month earlier than first planned; its operations page still describes an "impulsive rendezvous" in October, and secondary reports put the braking burns in late October. The app has Hera reaching Didymos on 12 October, before today, so it already shows Hera in orbit.

s.t: ESA: Hera targets early arrival at Didymos
Space.com: Hera on course for November rendezvous

e.from: waypoint 2026-10-12 "Rendezvous with Didymos"
e.to: waypoint date 2026-11-01 (ESA: "November 2026"; exact day not published)

sug.why: Changed by hand in trajectory.waypoints. Replace with the real date once ESA announces arrival.

c.q: Swift is still operating; it re-enters on 1 January 2027 (status_timeline)
c.note: NASA and Katalyst called off the reboost on 19 August 2026 after Katalyst’s LINK spacecraft lost attitude control. NASA says Swift will likely re-enter later in 2026; no date has been published. Most science operations were paused in February 2026 to slow the decay.

s.t: SpacePolicyOnline: No-go for Katalyst reboost of Swift
Nature World News: Swift will likely re-enter this year

e.from: The mission has been operating for over 20 years, contributing significantly to our understanding of black hole formation and neutron star mergers.
e.to: Over more than 20 years it has transformed our understanding of black hole formation and neutron star mergers. With its orbit decaying faster than expected, a commercial mission to boost it was called off in August 2026, and Swift is expected to re-enter the atmosphere by the end of the year.

sug.why: The status_timeline date (2027-01-01 → Re-entered) stays as a placeholder; set the real date when NASA announces it.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: From 2014 to 2019, under contract to JPL, our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) characterised, designed and tested the EM-CCD sensor for Roman’s coronagraph, leading to the CCD311 chosen for flight: a radiation-hardened version of the CCD201. We continue to refine the ‘trap-pumping’ techniques we developed for Euclid to counter radiation damage to these sensors.

c.q: Launched 19 May 2026 (Vega-C)
c.note: Confirmed: launched 03:52 UTC on 19 May 2026 from Kourou on Vega-C (one secondary source; ESA pages agree on the May launch).

We’re now part of the mission’s operations team, working with the imager’s team to get the most science from the detectors.

c.q: Mercury orbit insertion 21 November 2026
c.note: Still planned for 21 November 2026; the two orbiters separate on 9–10 December and the MPO reaches its science orbit in March 2027.

s.t: EPSC 2026 session TP18: BepiColombo nears Mercury

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We were on BepiColombo’s M-CAM monitoring camera team, analysing images from its Mercury flybys, and have led ESA’s Mercury Surface and Composition Working Group. With instrument lead the University of Leicester, we helped build the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS). Our scientists are now Co-Investigators on MIXS and on MERTIS, the Mercury Thermal Infrared Spectrometer, and associates on SIMBIO-SYS, the orbiter’s imaging and spectrometer system.

c.q: Snappier text
c.note: Shorter; same facts.

e.to: BepiColombo, a joint ESA-JAXA mission, is due to enter orbit around Mercury on 21 November 2026 and to be fully commissioned by April 2027. Its two orbiters will make the most complete study yet of Mercury’s surface, composition and magnetic field, mapping it at many wavelengths to explain the planet’s oversized core and its richness in volatile materials. The model shows the moment JAXA’s Mio orbiter is released; after that, the MOSIF sunshield separates and ESA’s Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) flies free.

c.q: Earth flyby 2026-09-28
c.note: Confirmed: closest approach over the Indian Ocean on 28 September 2026 at 11:45 UTC, about 8,640 km up. Next: Earth again in January 2029, then Jupiter in July 2031.

s.t: Sky at Night: Juice Earth flyby, 28 September 2026

s.t: OU news: the JANUS camera on JUICE

Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) also works on the detectors’ performance, calibration and radiation tolerance, and our robotic telescopes could follow up candidate stars once PLATO is flying.

c.q: Hayabusa2 "was" a mission; status En Route
c.note: The description is all in the past tense, but the spacecraft is on an extended mission (Hayabusa2#): it flew past asteroid Torifune on 5 July 2026 and is due at the 11-metre asteroid 1998 KY26 in 2031, after Earth flybys in 2027 and 2028.

e.from: The mission provided invaluable insights into the composition of carbon-rich asteroids and the history of the early Solar System.
e.to: The mission provided invaluable insights into the composition of carbon-rich asteroids and the history of the early Solar System. The spacecraft is now on an extended mission: it flew past asteroid Torifune on 5 July 2026 and is due to reach the tiny asteroid 1998 KY26 in 2031.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We’re developing EMS-L, the Exospheric Mass Spectrometer for LUPEX, an ESA instrument on the JAXA-ISRO rover. Building on our heritage in miniature ion-trap mass spectrometry, it will measure water and other volatiles in the thin lunar exosphere and those released as the rover drives and drills, to show how volatiles are spread and behave at the Moon’s south pole.

c.q: Snappier text
c.note: Shorter; same facts.

e.to: LUPEX is a joint JAXA-ISRO mission to look for water and other resources at the Moon’s south pole. Due to launch no earlier than 2028, its rover will explore sites with different lighting, temperatures and geology, measuring how much water there is, where, and in what form, down to about 1.5 metres. It should work for about 3.5 months after landing, and possibly for up to a year.

e.to: Our researchers were on the NASA/ESA Mars Sample Return Campaign Science Group and worked on planetary protection, planning how best to bring Perseverance’s Jezero Crater samples to Earth and analyse them. We also use the rover’s images and remote sensing to study the minerals of the ancient river delta, including clays and carbonates formed by water, and share this research with our students.

c.q: Lessons from Beagle 2 informed later landers including ExoMars
c.note: Still no source found (flagged since 2026-09-30).

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed. Includes the ESS correction.

e.to: Beagle 2 was conceived and led by our own Colin Pillinger, and we designed its Gas Analysis Package (GAP): a miniaturised mass spectrometer with twelve ovens, built to detect isotopic signs of past life in Martian soil. Fitting a laboratory-scale instrument into a probe the size of a dinner plate took major feats of miniaturisation. Our scientists also worked on its Environmental Sensor Suite, which was to measure the weather and look for dust devils. Contact was lost after the 2003 landing, but the lessons learned informed later landers, including ExoMars.

e.to: Our Atmospheric Research and Space Exploration group is leading the design phase of HiRIME, the High-Resolution Imager for Mars Exploration, which will take detailed images of the Martian surface for geology. The same group also leads the Dust Environment Spectral Imager, which will image the whole of Mars about every 10 minutes to watch its atmosphere and dust storms.

e.to: One of our scientists, John Zarnecki, was Principal Investigator for the Surface Science Package (SSP), which made the first measurements on Titan’s surface: its density, temperature and physical state as Huygens landed. We have continued to lead analysis of this unique dataset to understand Titan’s surface and organic chemistry.

e.to: In April 2025 we became one of only seven institutions outside China chosen to borrow Chang’e-5 samples. In our laboratories we’re measuring the isotopes of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and noble gases in the grains, to test the giant-impact theory of the Moon’s origin and trace the history of volatiles in the Earth-Moon system.

c.q: OU astronomers lead research groups finding gravitational lenses in Euclid surveys
c.note: Now sourced: OU news names Stephen Serjeant and Ruby Pearce-Casey in the Euclid lens search, and the 2025 A&A CNN lens-finding paper has the OU as first affiliation.

s.t: OU news: Euclid mission reveals spectacular new space discoveries
A&A 696, A214 (2025): Euclid strong lenses with CNNs (OU first affiliation)

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) played a lead role in characterising the CCD273 detectors in Euclid’s VIS instrument, and developed ‘trap pumping’, now used in orbit. It pinpoints individual radiation-damage defects in the detectors to within a fraction of a pixel, so images can be corrected and kept precise enough to trace dark matter through gravitational lensing. Our astronomers also lead searches of Euclid’s surveys for rare gravitational lenses.

c.q: OU supports agencies in selecting landing sites
c.note: Now sourced for ExoMars: OU researchers (Balme, Fawdon) were on the Oxia Planum selection paper and lead its geological mapping. Sample-return site selection still has no source.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We have a long history of Mars research, from building lander instruments to analysing atmospheric data from orbit. Our researchers study the planet’s volatile cycles and whether its subsurface could be habitable, and help space agencies choose landing sites, as for the Rosalind Franklin rover at Oxia Planum.

c.q: Ocean chemistry and habitability over time (added today)
c.note: OU conference abstracts by Sym, Ramkissoon, Fox-Powell, Pearson and Melwani Daswani; not yet a peer-reviewed paper.

s.t: ORO 95401: Composition and habitability of Europa’s ocean over time

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our astrobiologists study Europa as one of the Solar System’s most promising ocean worlds. We develop new cryogenic laboratory techniques and simulation facilities to study icy surface materials down to the microscale, and our fieldwork in polar places such as the Canadian High Arctic shows how ice and salts brought to the surface by cryovolcanism can reveal conditions in the ocean far below. We also model how the ocean’s chemistry, and how habitable it is, may have changed over 4.5 billion years as the water reacted with the rock beneath.

c.q: OU astrobiologists study Titan as an ocean world
c.note: Searched again today; still no public source.

c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Titan’s first global geomorphological map, published in Nature Astronomy in 2019, used Cassini data to identify six major terrain types, from plains to dune fields. Our astrobiologists study Titan as one of the icy ocean worlds, exploring how its surface chemistry and methane cycle relate to conditions for life.

e.to: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) tests how radiation damages the Teledyne e2v CIS120 CMOS sensor, which is being evaluated for TRUTHS and other next-generation missions. We measure its dark current, noise and sensitivity before and after gamma and proton irradiation, at a range of temperatures, to check it can keep the high calibration accuracy TRUTHS needs over a multi-year mission.

e.to: Part of our teaching, the Mars Yard lets students drive robotic rovers across a simulated Martian landscape from their own homes, making space science hands-on for learners anywhere.

c.q: OU machine learning on satellite imagery
c.note: Searched again today; still no public source.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We use Earth observation data to monitor environmental change, developing machine learning to track deforestation, urban growth and glacial retreat in satellite images. The work also feeds our teaching on technology and environmental sustainability.

c.q: OU use of the Hubble archive
c.note: Searched again today; still no public source.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our astronomers use Hubble’s archive to study stellar populations and how distant galaxies evolve, and the work feeds into our astronomy teaching. The CCDs in Hubble’s WFC3 camera were built by Teledyne e2v, the UK company that partners with our Centre for Electronic Imaging on testing and radiation-hardening space detectors.

c.q: OU cosmology with Planck and Euclid
c.note: Searched again today; still no public source.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We use Planck’s maps of the cosmic microwave background to study the large-scale structure of the early Universe and how galaxy clusters are spread. Our cosmologists combine Planck’s data with newer missions such as Euclid to research dark matter and dark energy, and it underpins our teaching of cosmology.

c.q: OU uses L2 as a virtual laboratory
c.note: Searched again today; still no public source.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We treat L2 as a natural laboratory for how deep space affects spacecraft components, following the performance of detectors we characterised for missions stationed there. What we learn improves the detectors we’re developing for future flagship missions.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We helped choose where OSIRIS-REx sampled Bennu, and we’re analysing the material it brought back to Earth (see OSIRIS-REx).

c.q: rate 0.2709

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) developed and tested the X-ray camera detectors on SMILE, the ESA–CAS mission studying how the solar wind meets Earth’s magnetic field. How particles from the Sun damage detectors in space is one of the CEI’s core research areas, and we test detectors against space radiation for missions across the Solar System.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We have studied Mercury’s surface composition for decades, using spectroscopy of data from visiting spacecraft to map its chemical elements and trace the planet’s early volcanic history. Our scientists are Co-Investigators on BepiColombo’s MIXS X-ray spectrometer, which will map the elements on its surface.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We’re helping to prepare ESA’s EnVision mission to Venus. With a £2.3 million ESA grant, our team leads the testing of the detectors in the VenSpec-U ultraviolet spectrometer, which will study the sulphur chemistry of Venus’s clouds, and we take part in the mission’s science preparations.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our scientists took part in BIOMEX, a DLR-led experiment outside the ISS that exposed bacteria, algae, lichens and fungi to the vacuum, UV radiation and temperature extremes of space for about 18 months. The samples came home with British astronaut Tim Peake in June 2016, and the results helped show whether such organisms (and, by extension, life on Mars) could survive travelling between planets.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) won £2.1 million to lead the testing and space qualification of the CIS303 and CIS120 UV detectors, built by Teledyne e2v, for CASTOR, a Canadian-led 1-metre UV/optical telescope targeting launch around 2030. We test and optimise the detectors, and measure how well different UV coatings work and how they degrade, to get the sensors ready for spaceflight.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our Compact CMOS Camera Demonstrator (C3D) won one of only three science payload slots on UKube-1, the UK Space Agency’s first CubeSat. Launched in July 2014, its three cameras made the first in-orbit demonstration of a European 0.18-micron CMOS imaging technology. Radiation testing showed the sensor degrading much like a CCD, along with effects unique to CMOS such as single-event upsets, and the data has since informed the design of more radiation-tolerant space CMOS sensors.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our analysis of Apollo samples helped show that the Moon is not as dry as once thought: water is locked inside lunar minerals. Drawing on instruments we built for Beagle 2 and Rosetta, we now develop miniature laboratories to measure what the Moon is made of. We also study how lunar soil could supply water, oxygen and fuel, and be used to build on the Moon, to support sustainable exploration.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) assessed how protons would damage the 24 CCD54 X-ray detectors in the C1XS instrument, modelling the shielding, temperature and voltages they needed. We tested 14 candidate detector modules before launch, recommended the ten best for flight, and advised on how the detectors coped with radiation in orbit.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our astronomers use JWST to study the atmospheres of planets around other stars. We were part of the international teams that analysed JWST’s first detailed observations of the giant planet WASP-39b, revealing its clouds and chemistry, and research we funded has studied the small rocky planet L 98-59 d, where JWST found possible signs of volcanic gases.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Before launch, our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) modelled how radiation damage would trap charge in Gaia’s CCDs, and we’ve since analysed its in-flight radiation data for the mission’s data processing. Gaia’s detectors turned out less damaged than ground tests predicted, a puzzle we’re still investigating to improve how future missions are tested. Our PhD students use Gaia’s catalogues to study star clusters and binary stars, our researchers use its alerts to find transient objects, and students on our S818 Space Science module follow up Gaia targets with our remote telescope in Tenerife.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) is developing low-noise UV and photon-counting detectors for HWO’s faint imaging, building on our CASTOR work. We’re also part of the UK consortium awarded £3 million in 2026 to develop one of the telescope’s core instruments.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We designed and led the development of UVIS, the ultraviolet channel of TGO’s NOMAD spectrometer, and one of our planetary scientists is a Co-Principal Investigator for NOMAD. We also help operate the CaSSIS stereo camera. We use UVIS data to track ozone, water vapour and trace gases such as methane, to understand how Mars loses its water to space. Some measurements are timed with other spacecraft: TGO measures methane from orbit while Curiosity measures it on the ground.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our academics are on Curiosity’s science and operations teams, focusing on noble gases and on how Martian rocks reacted with ancient water, which bears on whether Mars was habitable. Others combine the rover’s weather data with ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter observations to model Mars’s dust and water cycles.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) helped develop and tested the image sensor in JANUS, the camera on ESA’s JUICE mission, which will study Ganymede from orbit.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We helped calibrate Cassini’s Cosmic Dust Analyser and studied the composition of dust around Saturn. One of our scientists, John Zarnecki, led the Surface Science Package on the Huygens probe, which landed on Titan, Saturn’s largest moon.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our planetary scientists use Cassini’s datasets to study the habitability and chemistry of Saturn’s icy moons. We helped calibrate its Cosmic Dust Analyser and studied the dust around Saturn, and we still use Cassini’s archive to train students in planetary science.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: With RAL Space, we co-developed Ptolemy, the gas analyser on the Philae lander that measured the isotopes of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen in the comet. We also contributed to the MUPUS and GIADA instruments, coordinated the mission’s worldwide campaign of ground-based observations, and have explored why comet 67P’s dust and gas jets follow a day-night cycle.

c.q: Snappier text
c.note: Shorter; same facts.

e.to: ESA’s Rosetta made the first long-term study of a comet’s nucleus, orbiting Comet 67P for over two years as it travelled through the inner Solar System. Its lander, Philae, studied the surface directly, giving ground truth for the orbiter’s measurements. Together they revealed the physical and chemical make-up of comets and their possible part in the origin of life.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: With RAL Space, we designed and built the Ptolemy gas analyser, which with the COSAC instrument made the first analysis of organic matter on a comet’s surface. Our academics lead the interpretation of its data in the search for life’s chemical building blocks, work that has made our name in miniature planetary laboratories and comet science.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We were one of the international partners on JAXA’s AKARI infrared satellite, alongside Nagoya University, the University of Tokyo, ESA and other UK institutions. We used its all-sky infrared survey and spectra to study interstellar dust, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons and the earliest star formation in galaxies: part of the cosmic chemical cycle that eventually leads to habitable worlds.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our scientists analyse Spitzer’s archived light curves to study the atmospheres and orbits of transiting exoplanets, and use the data to teach infrared astronomy and the search for habitable worlds. The work also helps choose targets for new missions such as Ariel.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our astronomers used data from SPIRE, the camera and spectrometer built for Herschel by an international consortium led by Cardiff University, to study distant galaxies at sub-millimetre wavelengths and trace the history of star formation.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We proposed and developed the Exospheric Mass Spectrometer (EMS), Europe’s contribution to NASA’s PITMS instrument, with ESA funding and RAL Space, on a fast track to meet a tight budget and timescale. It was built to measure the Moon’s thin exosphere and how it changes over the lunar day and with the lander’s own effects. When Peregrine couldn’t land, we ran EMS in space to help diagnose the spacecraft, proving the technology ready to fly again on PROSPECT.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We’re a Co-Investigator institution for DISC, the instrument that will measure the size, mass and speed of dust particles as the spacecraft flies past its comet. Our Light-Gas Gun fires particles at several kilometres per second to check DISC’s dust shield can survive real high-speed impacts.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our Atmospheric Research and Space Exploration group leads the testing of the UV detectors for VenSpec-U, part of EnVision’s VenSpec suite, with a £2.3 million ESA grant. We also take part in the mission’s science preparations ahead of its launch in the early 2030s.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our Centre for Electronic Imaging (CEI) characterises and optimises the four EM-CCD sensors in OGRE’s X-ray camera, built by the UK company XCAM to survive the violent vibrations of launch. We research radiation damage, charge transfer and photon counting with these fast detectors for soft X-ray astronomy.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We worked with the OSIRIS-REx team to help choose Bennu’s Nightingale sample site, predicting surface temperatures so the spacecraft and samples wouldn’t overheat during collection. We’re also analysing the returned Bennu material to learn about the early Solar System’s chemistry and the origin of Earth’s water and organic molecules.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We were among the first in the world to analyse material from Stardust, using infrared, UV/visible and Raman spectroscopy to study the minerals in dust grains captured from Comet Wild 2 in aerogel. With studies of the samples’ organic content, this work made us a leading UK centre for comet sample science.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our oxygen isotope laboratory is one of the international groups analysing Ryugu samples returned by JAXA’s Hayabusa2 (see Hayabusa2).

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: Our scientists were on the Genesis Science Team. We developed some of the collectors that captured the solar wind and new techniques to analyse the returned samples, and after the capsule’s crash landing we worked extensively to characterise and clean off the contamination. The contamination stopped us making meaningful measurements, but Genesis’s finding that the Sun is richer in oxygen-16 than the Earth, Moon, Mars and meteorites is a key reference point for our oxygen isotope research.

c.q: OU text in the first person, snappier
c.note: First person ("we" is the OU) and shorter. Same facts; filler removed.

e.to: We own and run these telescopes, a cornerstone of our distance-learning astronomy teaching. Our academics use them to monitor variable stars and to support space missions such as Ariel from the ground, and students use them to gain real experience of collecting and analysing astronomical data.
